I am 70 years old, and I have worked this land for half a century. My bones ache in the morning, but I still know every inch of my three mu. My son and his wife work in the factory in Handan, so it is mostly me, my wife, and my grandson at home during the busy season. The boy helps when school allows. With seven mouths to feed, I cannot afford to gamble on strange crops. Cotton has been good to us. The soil here in Quzhou is suitable for it, and I have a well for irrigation when the rains fail, which they often do.

This year, I will plant all three mu with cotton, just like last year and the year before. I will go to the seed supply station and buy the improved cotton seeds that my neighbors and I have been using—Xinmian or something similar. The traditional seeds are not worth it anymore; the bollworm eats them, and the yield is too low. I will rotary till the field in mid-April to break up the soil and warm it up. I know that ploughing too deep is a waste of diesel and time at my age.

For fertilizer, I will apply about 15 jin of urea per mu as nitrogen, plus some diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride. Over my lifetime, I have learned that cotton is hungry during flowering and boll-setting. I will split the nitrogen—some at planting, some at flowering. I figure about 15 kg of pure nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 8 kg of potassium. I have learned this from watching the plants; when the leaves turn light green, they need more food.

Irrigation is expensive because pumping from the well costs electricity, but I will water three times: once at planting to help germination, once at early flowering in July when the heat comes, and once at peak boll formation in August. Any more is a waste of money, and the well water is not unlimited. 

Pests are the enemy. The bollworm always comes. I will spray pesticides four times this year—prevention is better than cure. I start before the eggs hatch, then hit them again at flowering. I do not use the most expensive chemicals; I use what the county extension recommends, rotated so the worms do not build resistance.

I expect to harvest about 110 kg of seed cotton per mu if the weather cooperates and the bollworm does not win. That is enough to pay for inputs, help with my grandson's school fees, and have a little left for my wife's medicine.
